Week 3: Solid results & guidance, 2026 
optimism intact
Tracking a 6%* EPS beat at halftime 
Following week 3, results from 167 S&P 500 companies (~50% of index earnings) are 
now in. Reported earnings came in 6% ahead of consensus *excluding Boeing’s one-time 
gain from an asset sale. 69% of companies beat on EPS, 63% on revenue and 51% on 
both – all metrics are below last quarter (76%/76%/63%) but above the week 3 avg. 
(65%/60%/46%). 4Q EPS growth (blended measure of actuals & consensus estimates) is 
now tracking 11% YoY (up from 7% last week), pushing the index toward its fifth 
consecutive quarter of double-digit EPS growth. 
Upbeat commentary; guidance off peak but still strong 
Corporate sentiment based on an NLP analysis of transcripts is tracking at a record high 
in 4Q, now above pre-Liberation Day levels of optimism (Exhibit 24); similarly, “weak 
demand” mentions are trending lower (Exhibit 25), and guidance improved last week 
after starting off cautious (see Week 2 recap) – there were 1.2x more above- than 
below-consensus EPS guides in Jan., a decline from the 1.9x we saw in the prior three 
months but much better than the Jan. avg. of 0.6x. Consensus 2026 S&P 500 EPS of 
$312 (+14% YoY) has held steady YTD, revised higher by 0.2% since Jan 1. 
AI’s “show me” moment splits hyperscalers 
Hyperscalers’ divergent price action after posting beats (Meta up 10%, Microsoft down 
10%) underscores AI’s transition from “tell me” to “show me”: beats without clear 
progress on AI monetization aren’t rewarded for upping capex. Meta’s above-consensus 
revenue guide, plus indications of AI driving usage and ad efficiencies, were enough for 
investors to feel comfortable with the above-consensus capex guide (see META recap). 
But Microsoft’s underwhelming Azure growth failed to dispel concerns (see MSFT recap). 
Muted reactions to beats/misses: guidance driving alpha 
Companies that beat on EPS and revenue have not seen as big of a pop as usual this 
quarter, but companies that missed have not sold off as much either (see Exhibit 9). 
Guidance has been a much stronger driver of price action, such that companies that 
issued above-consensus EPS guidance outperforming the S&P 500 by 410bp the next 
day (6x the reward for top- and bottom-line beats) whereas companies issuing below-
consensus EPS guidance lagged by 320bp (2x the penalty for misses). 
Up next: the busiest week of earnings (130 companies) 
130 companies representing 25% of index earnings are slated to report this week. By 
Friday, 75% of earnings will be in. Big tech earnings continue with Google (Wednesday) 
and Amazon (Thursday). So far, the sector has exceeded the high expectations set for it 
– Tech + Mag 7 earnings are tracking +24% YoY in 4Q, up from the projected 20%
heading into reporting season.

 4Q25 Earnings: Week 3 
Earnings transcript commentary 
Tech 
• 
Meta (Interactive Media) – “We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance 
leases to be in the range of $115 billion to $135 billion [vs. consensus at $110bn], with year-over-year growth 
driven by increased investment to support our Meta Superintelligence Labs efforts and core business. Despite the 
meaningful step up in infrastructure investment, in 2026, we expect to deliver operating income that is above 2025 
operating income.” 
• 
Microsoft (Software) – “Capital expenditures were $37.5 billion [vs. consensus $36.3 billion], and this quarter, roughly 
two-thirds of our CapEx was on short-lived assets, primarily GPUs and CPUs. Our customer demand continues to 
exceed our supply.” 
• 
Apple (Tech Hardware) – “First of all, we were thrilled with the customer response on the latest iPhone lineup. It 
exceeded our expectations to say the least. And iPhone grew 23%. What the result of that was, was that we exited the 
December quarter with very lean channel inventory due to that staggering level of demand. And based on that, we're in a 
supply chase mode to meet the very high levels of customer demand. We're currently constrained. And at this 
point, it's difficult to predict when supply and demand will balance.” 
• 
ASML (Semi Equipment) – “The market outlook has improved notably over the last months, especially as related 
to the continued buildup of data centers and AI-related infrastructure. This buildup is now translated into additional 
capacity needs at our advanced Logic and DRAM customers, and in turn, an increased demand across our product portfolio, 
especially in our EUV business.” 
• 
Seagate (Tech Hardware) – We continue to operate in an exceptionally strong demand environment, particularly within 
the data center end markets…Based on our build-to-order pipeline, we anticipate these positive demand trends will 
continue for some time.” 
Consumer 
• 
Mastercard (Financial Services) – “If you zoom out and you look across the world, these patterns are different by region 
here and there, but the aggregate top-line is the consumer spending remains healthy is the same.” 
• 
Visa (Financial Services) – “Growth across consumer spend bands remained relatively consistent with Q4, with 
the highest spend band continuing to grow the fastest. We did not see a deterioration in the lower spend band, 
and across our volume, both discretionary and non-discretionary spend remained strong.” 
Labor 
• 
ManpowerGroup (HR & Employment Services) – “It is true that AI will impact most jobs, most skills inside most jobs. 
The difference? It will be to varying degrees...What we found is that for blue collar industrial manufacturing roles, 
they appear to be more resilient over the horizon where the disruption is happening more in the white-collar 
software developers and coders, as we've already seen, in demand. You know, keep in mind, though, that in the US, 
software developers are still the number three job in demand in our country. So even though it's impacted, it's still a huge, 
in-demand role. We've also seen impact in call center professionals.” 
• 
Automatic Data Processing (HR & Employment Services) – Q: “Any updated views on [layoff announcements] and 
impacts that AI could be having on the broader labor market?” A: “I think more of the headlines I've seen actually 
have been more about sort of corporate realignment following a big hiring period post-pandemic…We look at it 
by industry, about 10 or 12 industry groups. We're not really seeing anything discernible there… things like financial 
services, things like professional services, tech, and so on, we're actually seeing reasonably healthy growth. So, it's hard 
to say, but the data, the empirical data does not really point to that happening at this point in time.”

Muted reactions to beats & misses: guidance driving alpha 
Companies that beat on both the top and bottom line have outperformed the S&P 500 
by an avg. of 70bp the next day, an improvement from last week (beats were 
underperforming by an average of 40bp as of week 2), but still well below the historical 
avg. outperformance of 140bp. Companies that missed on both EPS and revenue have 
also seen muted reactions, underperforming by an average of 160bp vs. the historical 
average of 250bp. Guidance has been a larger driver of returns, with companies that 
issued above-consensus EPS guidance outperforming by 410bp on average vs. -320bp 
for those that issued below-consensus guidance.

AI arms race alive and well 
Hyperscalers (MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, META, ORCL) have showed no signs of pulling back 
on the AI capex cycle despite increased scrutiny. Divergent price action last week (Meta 
up 10%, Microsoft down 10%) underscores AI’s transition from “tell me” to “show me”, 
where beats without clear progress on AI monetization aren’t likely to be rewarded. 
Meta’s above-consensus revenue guide, plus indications of AI driving usage and ad 
efficiencies, were enough for investors to feel comfortable with the above-consensus 
capex guide (see META recap). But Microsoft’s underwhelming Azure growth did not 
dispel concerns (see MSFT recap). Overall, hyperscalers are expected to spend a 
combined $410bn in 2025 and $550bn in 2026.

Capex cycle slated to remain strong 
Capex grew by >20% YoY in 2Q and 3Q and is forecast to post similar growth in 4Q (see 
Exhibit 15). AI has been the primary driver of the capex cycle so far but spend could 
broaden out to other sectors from here given bi-partisan support for reshoring and 
manufacturing in the US, plus an incremental boost from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act 
(OBBBA). Tariff uncertainty likely paused projects, translating to pent-up activity in the 
pipeline.

Our economists argue that if the IEEPA (International Emergency Economic Power Act) 
tariffs are struck down, the net effect on economic activity would likely be positive but 
depends on i) the extent to which policy uncertainty increases as the administration

put in place for a maximum of 150 days). Our economists’ base case is for the effective

Appendix - Methodology 
Guidance Ratios 
Earnings guidance: We track the number of instances of above- vs. below-consensus 
management guidance for earnings over the last three months for S&P 500 companies. 
If a company issues changes to its outlook more than once in a one-month period, we 
incorporate all instances of guidance into our aggregate number. The ratio also includes 
all instances of above- or below-consensus earnings guidance issued by a company (for 
example, if they issue both quarterly and annual guidance). The one-month and three-
month revision ratios are calculated as they are for estimate revision ratios. The data 
source is Bloomberg. For companies that provide both GAAP and Operating guidance, or 
for REITs that provide both EPS and FFO guidance, we remove one data point if both 
data points provide the same guidance direction, otherwise both data points are used. 
Capex guidance: We track the number of instances of above- vs. below-consensus 
management guidance for planned capex over the last three months for S&P 500 
companies, calculated the same way as above; data source is FactSet. 
 
Earnings Revision ratios 
Beginning in April 1986 (and January 2006 for Real Estate), we calculate the ratio 
between the number of companies in the S&P 500 for which Thomson Financial 
consensus earnings estimates have been raised versus those that have been lowered. 
We apply the same calculation to the S&P 500 GICS Sectors (where we use FFO for 
REITs within Real Estate). One-month revision ratios are computed as the number of 
companies for which estimates this month are higher than they were last month, divided 
by the number of companies for which estimates this month are lower than they were 
last month. For example, within a particular subgroup of the market, if consensus 
estimates have increased for 5 companies and have decreased for 10, the estimate 
revision ratio will be 0.5 (5 divided by 10). 
The three-month revision ratio is similarly defined as the total number of earnings 
estimate increases divided by total number of earnings estimate decreases during the 
last three months. For example, in February 2002, the three-month revision ratio is 
computed as the total number of companies with increased monthly estimates, divided 
by the total number of companies with decreased estimates throughout December 2001, 
January 2002, and February 2002. 
We similarly calculate the S&P 600 (small cap) earnings revision ratios (one-month and 
three-month) by the same methodology, with data beginning in February 2001. 
For earnings/sales estimates, we look at the change in the FY1 estimate (current 
unreported year) if there's more than 120 days between the current date and the 
company's fiscal year-end date, otherwise we look at the change in the FY2 estimate 
(next unreported year).

Methodology: Earnings Calls Sentiment 
With the help of BofA’s Predictive Analytics team, we parsed through earnings calls 
transcripts to calculate sentiment for the S&P500 universe of companies that have 
reported since 31st March 2020. We use the Loughran McDonald’s financial dictionary 
to calculate sentiment scores as per the definition below. 
Sentiment score = No. of Unique positive words – No. of unique negative and 
uncertainty words 
The sentiment score is computed with three different filters: the full transcript, 
management discussion and answers of CEO/CFO from Q/A section. Calculated scores 
were then averaged on the Sector level. Loughran-McDonald Sentiment and Uncertainty: 
1. 
Loughran-McDonald Sentiment: Examples of positive words include accomplish, 
achieve, outperform, stabilize, strength and negative words such as abandon, 
abnormal, downturn, evade, failing, stagnate. In total, the lexicon has 2,355 
negative words and 354 positive words. 
2. 
Loughran-McDonald Uncertainty: Examples of uncertain words include almost, 
ambiguity, hidden, fluctuate, doubts, unclear. In total, the lexicon has 297 words. 
Note that the charts show the sentiment score multiplied by (- 1) and after applying the 
natural log to normalize the data on the same scale. Our Predictive Analytics team is
